abstract: As a ubiquitous and essential posttranslational modification occurring in both plants and animals, protein N-linked glycosylation regulates various important biological processes. Unlike the well-studied animal N-glycoproteomes, the landscape of rice N-glycoproteome remains largely unexplored. Here, by developing a chemical glycoproteomic strategy based on metabolic glycan labeling, we report a comprehensive profiling of the N-glycoproteome in rice seedlings. The rice seedlings are incubated with N -azidoacetylgalactosamine—a monosaccharide analog containing a bioorthogonal functional group—to metabolically label N-glycans, followed by conjugation with an affinity probe via click chemistry for the enrichment of the N-glycoproteins. Subsequent mass spectrometry analyses identify a total of 403 N-glycosylation sites and 673 N-glycosylated proteins, which are involved in various important biological processes. In particular, the core components of the endoplasmic reticulum–associated protein degradation machinery are N-glycosylated, and the N-glycosylation is important for the endoplasmic reticulum–associated protein degradation-L function. This work not only provides an invaluable resource for studying rice N-glycosylation but also demonstrates the applicability of metabolic glycan labeling in glycoproteomic profiling for crop species.

Agrobacterium tumefaciens
injection. The HEK293T (ATCC CRL-11268) and HeLa (ATCC CCL-2) cell lines were acquired from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). All cells were cultured in a CO

2

Plasmid Construction
To construct His-tagged
OsUGE
expression plasmids in
Escherichia coli

OsUGE1
(LOC_Os05g51670) and
OsUGE2
(LOC_Os08g28730) were amplified and cloned into the pCold-TF vector (Takara). To validate the candidates of N-linked glycoproteins in rice, the coding sequences of each gene were amplified and cloned into the pCAMBIA1300 vector with a 3 × HA tag at the C-terminus. For the validation of N-linked glycoproteins and sites in rice, the WT coding sequences of each gene and the mutated sequences with asparagine residue converted to glutamine were chemically synthesized, with a Myc tag incorporated at the C-terminus. Subsequently, these sequences were ligated into the pCAMBIA2301 vector. The coding sequences of
Arabidopsis CPY
(AT3G10410) were chemically synthesized, introducing a G-to-R mutation at residue 227. An HA tag was incorporated at the N-terminus. Subsequently, these sequences were ligated into the pJL1460 vector. All primers used were listed in
Supplemental Table S1
.
Experimental Design and Statistics
For the identification of N-glycosylated proteins and sites, two sample groups (mock and GalNAz-labeled samples) were prepared, each with three biological replicates. Each 10 mg of GalNAz-labeled and unlabeled protein lysates was subjected separately to a click reaction with alkyne-biotin. After enrichment with streptavidin beads and on-beads trypsin digestion, each sample was divided into two fractions: the supernatant and pellets. The supernatant of the control and GalNAz-labeled samples was subjected to stable isotopic dimethyl labeling and mixed. Each sample was fractionated using an Agilent HPLC system into 14 individual fractions and then subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis, followed by searching with both MaxQuant and Thermo Proteome Discoverer. The proteins that appeared in at least two out of three biological replicates and had a minimum of two unique peptides were statistically analyzed using an empirical Bayes moderated
t
test implemented in the Limma package within R/Bioconductor (
29
). Proteins with a
p
-value ≤ 0.05 and a fold change ≥1.5 were reported as GalNAz-modified proteins. The pellets were digested with peptide-
N
-glycosidase F (PNGase F) and PNGase A to released glycopeptides, which were then subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis. The raw data of N-glycosylation sites were processed using the MaxQuant software. The peptides that exhibited both deamidation and nondeamidation after PNGase elution were considered as nonspecific adsorption to the beads, were not regarded as N-glycosylation sites, and were removed from the analysis. The sites with location probability ≥0.75, score ≥40, ΔScore ≥6 were considered unambiguous N-glycosylation sites.
Search Parameters
The data processing of dimethylated reductive was conducted using Thermo Proteome Discoverer 2.4 software. The analysis utilized the
O. sativa
L. proteome database, which was downloaded from MSU on July 4th, 2017, and contains 66,338 protein entries. Database search was performed with the following parameters: allowing for two trypsin missed cleavage sites, using precursor and fragment mass tolerances of 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively; carbamidomethyl (Cys), dimethyl labeling (N-terminus), and dimethyl labeling (Lys) were chosen as static modifications with tag masses of +28.03130 Da (light, mock) and +34.06312 Da (heavy, GalNAz labeling), respectively. Oxidation (Met, 15.995 Da) was selected as a variable modification. The false discovery rate (FDR) for peptide identification was calculated using the Percolator algorithm in the Proteome Discoverer workflow based on the search results against a decoy database and was set at 1% FDR. The abundances extracted from MS1 spectra of each identified peptide peaks were used to calculate the relative ratio, subsequently.
The data processing of dimethylated reductive was conducted using the MaxQuant software environment (version 1.6.1.10). Database search was performed with the following parameters: trypsin/P was chosen as digestion mode with a maximum of two missed cleavages. The minimal peptide length was set to six amino acids. Two multiplicity labels with DimethNter0 and DimethLys0 were chosen as Light labels, and DimethNter6 and DimethLys6 were chosen as Heavy labels. Methionine oxidation and acetyl N-terminus were set as variable, while carbamidomethyl cysteine was set as a fixed modification. For first search and main search, the maximal mass tolerance was set to 20 ppm and 4.5 ppm, respectively. The FDR for protein identification was set to 0.01, and at least two unique peptides were required. The “re-quantify” and “match between runs” were enabled, and only proteins with at least two quantified peptides were reported as quantified proteins.
The raw data of N-glycosylation sites were processed using the MaxQuant software environment. The
O. sativa
L. proteome database was employed for both full MS and tandem MS/MS searches, utilizing the Andromeda search engine integrated within the MaxQuant framework. The following parameters were set for the database search: a precursor mass tolerance of 20 ppm for the initial search and 4.5 ppm for the main search, with a fragment mass tolerance of 20 ppm. Enzyme digestion was performed using trypsin with allowance for up to two missed cleavages, and the minimum peptide length was set to seven amino acids. An FDR of 0.01 was applied to filter proteins and peptides. Asn-Asp was considered as a variable modification, while carbamidomethyl was selected as a fixed modification. For the identification of nonenzymatic deamidation sites, the raw data were processed using the MaxQuant software environment, and the search parameters were identical to those used for N-glycosylation site identification as mentioned above.

Induced Fit Docking
The input structure underwent a standard process in the Protein Preparation Wizard panel of Schrödinger Maestro (
30

Total RNA was extracted from materials using TRIzol, followed by treatment with TURBO DNase to remove genomic DNA contamination. Detection of Artificial Cysteine S-glycosylation
Detection of S-glycosylation was performed following the methodology described in a previous study (
35

The tissue was then homogenized using lysis buffer composed of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1% NP-40, and a complete protease inhibitor cocktail. After centrifugation at 4 °C (20,000
g

Fifty microliter of the cell lysate was incubated with 2 mM of the corresponding unnatural monosaccharide at 37 °C for a duration of 2 h. Following the incubation, the reaction samples were precipitated by adding 500 μl of methanol and incubating at −80 °C for 1 h. The precipitated proteins were then centrifuged at 8000
g
for 5 min at 4 °C and washed twice with 500 μl of cold methanol. The resulting pellet was resuspended in PBS buffer containing 0.5% SDS, which was subsequently used for the subsequent click reaction as described above. The reaction samples were separated using a 10% SDS-PAGE gel, and the labeling efficiency was assessed by detecting fluorescence signals within the gel.
Verification of N-Linked Glycoproteins
To validate the N-glycosylation modification of rice proteins in a plant expression system, the coding sequences of candidate rice protein genes were cloned into the binary vector pCAMBIA1300 with a 3 × HA tag. The constructed vectors were then transformed into
A. tumefaciens

A. tumefaciens

2

600
= 0.7 and then injected into
N

benthamiana

Three milliliters of the powder were dissolved in lysis buffer containing 50 mM sodium phosphate (pH 7.0), 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1% NP-40, 1% SDS, 1% Triton, and a complete protease inhibitor cocktail. The lysate was precipitated with a methanol-chloroform solution and resuspended in 1 ml of PBS containing 1% SDS (w/v), resulting in a dilution of the SDS concentration to 0.5%. To the lysates, 40 mM DTT was added, making a total volume of 40 μl, and the mixture was boiled at 95 °C for 10 min. The lysate was then incubated at 37 °C with 1× glyco-buffer, 1 × NP-40, and 1 unit of PNGase A enzyme for 12 h. After cleavage, the samples were separated by 6% or 8% SDS-PAGE gel and detected using an HA tag antibody. To validate the N-glycosylation modification of proteins in mammalian cell lines, HEK293T and HeLa cell lysates were precipitated with a methanol-chloroform solution and resuspended in PBS containing 0.5% SDS (w/v), followed by digestion with PNGase F enzyme. The samples were separated by 6% or 8% SDS-PAGE gel and detected using endogenous protein antibodies.

Protein Sample Preparation
To assess the metabolic labeling efficiency, 14-day-old rice seedlings were cultivated in Kimura B nutrient solution supplemented with varying concentrations of the specified unnatural monosaccharides for a duration of 3 days. Following this, the seedlings were harvested and rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen. The frozen samples were then homogenized using a lysis buffer composed of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1% NP-40, 1% SDS, 1% Triton, and a complete protease inhibitor cocktail. After centrifugation, the resulting supernatants were precipitated with methanol-chloroform, and the protein pellets were resuspended in 50 μl PBS buffer containing 1% SDS. Protein quantification was performed using a BCA protein assay kit (Pierce) to normalize the lysates to a concentration of 5 mg/ml. For the click reaction, 0.5 mg of protein lysate, a premixed complex of 50 μM CuSO
4
-BTTAA (in a molar ratio of 1:2), 100 μM alkyne-probes, and 12.5 mM fresh sodium ascorbate were combined in a total volume of 50 μl, followed by incubation at 25 °C for 2 h. The reaction products were then subjected to in-gel fluorescence scanning using a Typhoon FLA 9500 Fluorescence Imager (GE Healthcare, Life Sciences). Additionally, Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining was performed to confirm equal loading of proteins.
For the PNGase A and PNGase F treatment assay of GalNAz-labeled samples, 14-day-old ZH11 seedlings were incubated with or without 10 mM GalNAz for 3 days, then lysed. The GalNAz-labeled samples were divided into two parts, one of which was treated with PNGase A and PNGase F for 12 h to release N-linked glycans. All samples were reacted with alkyne-biotin and then detected by immunoblot with streptavidin-HRP.
For mass spectrometry analysis, 10 mg of labeled and unlabeled protein lysates were separately subjected to a click reaction with alkyne-biotin. The resulting click reaction products were then precipitated using methanol-chloroform to remove any excess click reagents. The resulting pellets from the methanol-chloroform precipitation after the click reaction were re-suspended in 1.5 ml of PBS buffer containing 1.2% SDS. The concentration of SDS was subsequently diluted to 0.2% with PBS, and the samples were filtered through a 0.2-μm filter. Next, 150 μl of streptavidin agarose beads, which had been pre-washed, were added to the protein solution, followed by rotation for 4 h at room temperature. The beads were then washed sequentially with PBS (pH 7.4) and Milli-Q water five times to remove nonspecifically bound proteins. Subsequently, the beads were re-suspended in 500 μl of 6 M urea containing 10 mM DTT and incubated at 37 °C for more than 60 min. Afterward, 20 mM IAA was added and incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 45 min. The beads were washed with PBS, followed by centrifugation, and then re-suspended in 200 μl of triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer containing 1 M urea, 1 mM CaCl
2
, and 10 ng/μl trypsin. Trypsin digestion was performed on a rotary shaker for more than 18 h at 37 °C. After digestion, the supernatants were collected, and the beads were washed with 100 μl of Milli-Q water.

For the identification of N-glycosylated sites, the supernatants after trypsin digestion were removed, and the beads were washed sequentially with PBS (pH 7.4) and Milli-Q water five times. To release the modified peptides, the beads were eluted with 200 μl of 50 mM ABC and incubated with PNGase F and PNGase A for 12 h at 37 °C. After centrifugation, the eluents were collected, and the beads were washed with 200 μl of Milli-Q water two times. All the eluents were combined and dried in a vacuum rotary evaporator for LC-MS/MS analysis.
For the identification of nonenzymatic deamidation sites, 0.5 ml of frozen 14-day-old rice seedlings were homogenized as mentioned above. After centrifugation, the supernatants were precipitated with methanol-chloroform and re-suspended in 100 μl 6 M urea, with 10 mM DTT added. The samples were incubated at 37 °C for at least 60 min. Subsequently, 20 mM IAA was added, and the mixture was incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 45 min. The samples were then diluted to 0.6 M urea with 50 mM ABC (pH 7.4) and digested with trypsin (1:50) at 37 °C for 12 h. The samples were desalted and fractionated into eight portions using the Pierce High pH Reversed-Phase Peptide Fractionation Kit (catalog no.84868) and dried in a vacuum rotary evaporator for LC-MS/MS analysis.
LC-MS/MS Analysis
To identify GalNAz-labeled proteins and nonenzymatic deamidation sites, LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a 5 μm C18 bulk material packed loading column (100 μm × 2 cm), a separating C18 capillary column (75 μm × 10 cm) fused with 3 μm C18 resin, and an EASY-nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The prepared samples were reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid in water (vol/vol) and loaded onto the pre-column. Separation was achieved by eluting from the separating column using a gradient of 3 to 37% B [A: 0.1% formic acid in water (vol/vol), B: 0.1% formic acid in ACN (vol/vol)] over a 70-min period. Subsequently, HCD-based LC-MS/MS analysis was performed. Under positive ion mode, full-scan mass spectra were acquired over the m/z range from 300 to 2000 using the Orbitrap mass analyzer with the mass resolution setting of 70,000. MS/MS fragmentation was performed in data-dependent mode, selecting the 20 most intense ions from each full-scan mass spectrum for high-energy collision-induced dissociation and MS2 analysis. MS2 spectra were acquired using the Orbitrap analyzer at a resolution setting of 17,500. Other parameters, presented in the centroid format, included an isolation window of 2.0 m/z units, default charge of 2+, normalized collision energy of 28%, maximum injection time (IT) of 50 ms, and dynamic exclusion of 20.0 s.
To identify N-glycosylation sites, LC-MS/MS analysis was conducted for 3 h using an Orbitrap Fusion LUMOS Tribrid Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the HCD method. Peptides were separated using a loading column (100 μm × 2 cm) and an in-house packed C18 separating capillary column (75 μm × 15 cm) containing Luna 3 μm C18 bulk packing material (Phenomenex). The mobile phases (A: water with 0.1% formic acid, and B: 80% ACN with 0.1% formic acid) were delivered and controlled by a Dionex Ultimate 3000 RPLC nano system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The LC gradient began at 2% B for the initial 8 min, followed by an increase from 2% to 10% B from 8 to 9 min, a further increase from 10% to 44% B from 9 to 183 min, and finally an increase from 44% to 99% B from 183 to 188 min. For samples analyzed using the Orbitrap Fusion LUMOS Tribrid Mass Spectrometer, peptide precursors were ionized using an EASY-Spray ionization source (Thermo Fisher Scientific) held at +2.0 kV compared to ground, with the inlet capillary temperature maintained at 320 °C. Survey scans of peptide precursors were collected in the Orbitrap analyzer over the range of 350-1600 Th, with an AGC target of 400,000, maximum IT of 50 ms, RF lens at 30%, and a resolution of 60,000 at 200 m/z. Monoisotopic precursor selection was enabled for peptide isotopic distributions, and precursors of z = 2 to 7 were selected for data-dependent MS/MS scans, with a cycle time of 3 s. Dynamic exclusion was set to 15 s, with a ±10 ppm window set around the precursor monoisotope. During HCD scans, automated scan range determination was enabled. Precursor ions were isolated using a 1.6 Th window with the quadrupole, while product ions were collected in the Orbitrap with the first mass of 110 Th, an AGC target of 50,000, a maximum IT of 30 ms, HCD collision energy at 30%, and a resolution of 15,000.

body:
As one of the most abundant posttranslational modifications of proteins, glycosylation plays essential roles in various fundamental molecular and cellular processes (
1
,
2
,
3
). It is estimated that over 50% of the proteins in human cells undergo glycosylation (
4
), with the majority of secreted and membrane-bound proteins being N-linked glycosylated at asparagine (Asn) residues in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus during secretion (
5
). N-glycosylation is a prevalent type of protein glycosylation found in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes (
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
). In multicellular organisms, N-glycosylation is implicated in regulating developmental processes (
12
,
13
). Disruption of the biosynthesis of hybrid and complex N-glycans in mice results in embryonic lethality (
14
). Similarly, plants with mutations in genes encoding N-glycosylation enzymes display severe growth defects (
15
,
16
). Similar to other eukaryotic organisms, plants initiate protein N-glycosylation in the ER, where the lipid-linked oligosaccharide (Glc
3
Man
9
GlcNAc
2
) is transferred onto Asn of nascent polypeptides containing the consensus sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr (where X ≠ Pro) by oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) (
17
). Additionally, some Asn within the Asn-X-Cys sequences may also undergo N-glycosylation (
18
).
Glycoproteomic analysis of N-glycosylation has been widely performed in animal systems. N-glycoproteins and N-glycopeptides can be enriched by using techniques such as affinity-based strategies [
e.g.
, hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography] and chemical glycoproteomics [
e.g.
, metabolic glycan labeling (MGL)] (
19
,
20
). With complementarity, these two types of methods have facilitated uncovering the N-glycoproteomes in animals (
21
,
22
). In contrast, the N-glycoproteome landscape in plants remains much less explored. By using affinity-based strategies, N-glycoproteins and N-glycosylation sites have previously been identified in a variety of plants, including
Arabidopsis thaliana
, rice, tomato, and cotton (
23
,
24
,
25
,
26
,
27
,
28
). To further elucidate the plant N-glycoproteomes, it is therefore of great interest to explore the use of MGL for large-scale identification of N-glycosylated proteins and modification sites in plants. Previously, we have demonstrated that N-glycoproteins in
A. thaliana
could be labeled and enriched by using the MGL method (
10
).
In this work, we report the development of an MGL-based chemical glycoproteomic method for comprehensive profiling of the N-glycoproteome in rice. By incubation of the rice seedlings with
N
-azidoacetylgalactosamine (GalNAz), an unnatural sugar containing a bioorthogonal functional group, the N-glycans were metabolically incorporated with azides. Subsequent click reaction with an affinity tag allowed for the enrichment of N-glycoproteins for analysis by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). A total of 403 N-glycosylation sites and 673 N-glycosylated proteins were identified, which were involved in various important biological and pathological processes such as plant development, nutrition, ER protein processing, and interactions with pathogens. For example, N-glycosylation was implicated in the ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) pathway. Specifically, the core components of the ERAD-L machinery were N-glycosylated and the N-glycans play an important role in regulating the ERAD-L function. Our study provides an invaluable resource for studying the biological functions of N-glycosylation in rice and demonstrates the versatility of MGL in studying plant glycosylation.

Experimental Design and Statistics
For the identification of N-glycosylated proteins and sites, two sample groups (mock and GalNAz-labeled samples) were prepared, each with three biological replicates. Each 10 mg of GalNAz-labeled and unlabeled protein lysates was subjected separately to a click reaction with alkyne-biotin. After enrichment with streptavidin beads and on-beads trypsin digestion, each sample was divided into two fractions: the supernatant and pellets. The supernatant of the control and GalNAz-labeled samples was subjected to stable isotopic dimethyl labeling and mixed. Each sample was fractionated using an Agilent HPLC system into 14 individual fractions and then subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis, followed by searching with both MaxQuant and Thermo Proteome Discoverer. The proteins that appeared in at least two out of three biological replicates and had a minimum of two unique peptides were statistically analyzed using an empirical Bayes moderated
t
test implemented in the Limma package within R/Bioconductor (
29
). Proteins with a
p
-value ≤ 0.05 and a fold change ≥1.5 were reported as GalNAz-modified proteins. The pellets were digested with peptide-
N
-glycosidase F (PNGase F) and PNGase A to released glycopeptides, which were then subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis. The raw data of N-glycosylation sites were processed using the MaxQuant software. The peptides that exhibited both deamidation and nondeamidation after PNGase elution were considered as nonspecific adsorption to the beads, were not regarded as N-glycosylation sites, and were removed from the analysis. The sites with location probability ≥0.75, score ≥40, ΔScore ≥6 were considered unambiguous N-glycosylation sites.
Search Parameters
The data processing of dimethylated reductive was conducted using Thermo Proteome Discoverer 2.4 software. The analysis utilized the
O. sativa
L. proteome database, which was downloaded from MSU on July 4th, 2017, and contains 66,338 protein entries. Database search was performed with the following parameters: allowing for two trypsin missed cleavage sites, using precursor and fragment mass tolerances of 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively; carbamidomethyl (Cys), dimethyl labeling (N-terminus), and dimethyl labeling (Lys) were chosen as static modifications with tag masses of +28.03130 Da (light, mock) and +34.06312 Da (heavy, GalNAz labeling), respectively. Oxidation (Met, 15.995 Da) was selected as a variable modification. The false discovery rate (FDR) for peptide identification was calculated using the Percolator algorithm in the Proteome Discoverer workflow based on the search results against a decoy database and was set at 1% FDR. The abundances extracted from MS1 spectra of each identified peptide peaks were used to calculate the relative ratio, subsequently.
The data processing of dimethylated reductive was conducted using the MaxQuant software environment (version 1.6.1.10). Database search was performed with the following parameters: trypsin/P was chosen as digestion mode with a maximum of two missed cleavages. The minimal peptide length was set to six amino acids. Two multiplicity labels with DimethNter0 and DimethLys0 were chosen as Light labels, and DimethNter6 and DimethLys6 were chosen as Heavy labels. Methionine oxidation and acetyl N-terminus were set as variable, while carbamidomethyl cysteine was set as a fixed modification. For first search and main search, the maximal mass tolerance was set to 20 ppm and 4.5 ppm, respectively. The FDR for protein identification was set to 0.01, and at least two unique peptides were required. The “re-quantify” and “match between runs” were enabled, and only proteins with at least two quantified peptides were reported as quantified proteins.
The raw data of N-glycosylation sites were processed using the MaxQuant software environment. The
O. sativa
L. proteome database was employed for both full MS and tandem MS/MS searches, utilizing the Andromeda search engine integrated within the MaxQuant framework. The following parameters were set for the database search: a precursor mass tolerance of 20 ppm for the initial search and 4.5 ppm for the main search, with a fragment mass tolerance of 20 ppm. Enzyme digestion was performed using trypsin with allowance for up to two missed cleavages, and the minimum peptide length was set to seven amino acids. An FDR of 0.01 was applied to filter proteins and peptides. Asn-Asp was considered as a variable modification, while carbamidomethyl was selected as a fixed modification. For the identification of nonenzymatic deamidation sites, the raw data were processed using the MaxQuant software environment, and the search parameters were identical to those used for N-glycosylation site identification as mentioned above.

The frozen samples were then homogenized using a lysis buffer composed of 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1% NP-40, 1% SDS, 1% Triton, and a complete protease inhibitor cocktail. After centrifugation, the resulting supernatants were precipitated with methanol-chloroform, and the protein pellets were resuspended in 50 μl PBS buffer containing 1% SDS. For the PNGase A and PNGase F treatment assay of GalNAz-labeled samples, 14-day-old ZH11 seedlings were incubated with or without 10 mM GalNAz for 3 days, then lysed. The resulting click reaction products were then precipitated using methanol-chloroform to remove any excess click reagents. The resulting pellets from the methanol-chloroform precipitation after the click reaction were re-suspended in 1.5 ml of PBS buffer containing 1.2% SDS. The concentration of SDS was subsequently diluted to 0.2% with PBS, and the samples were filtered through a 0.2-μm filter. Next, 150 μl of streptavidin agarose beads, which had been pre-washed, were added to the protein solution, followed by rotation for 4 h at room temperature. The beads were then washed sequentially with PBS (pH 7.4) and Milli-Q water five times to remove nonspecifically bound proteins. Subsequently, the beads were re-suspended in 500 μl of 6 M urea containing 10 mM DTT and incubated at 37 °C for more than 60 min. Afterward, 20 mM IAA was added and incubated in the dark at 37 °C for 45 min. The beads were washed with PBS, followed by centrifugation, and then re-suspended in 200 μl of triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer containing 1 M urea, 1 mM CaCl
2

LC-MS/MS Analysis
To identify GalNAz-labeled proteins and nonenzymatic deamidation sites, LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a 5 μm C18 bulk material packed loading column (100 μm × 2 cm), a separating C18 capillary column (75 μm × 10 cm) fused with 3 μm C18 resin, and an EASY-nLC 1200 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The prepared samples were reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid in water (vol/vol) and loaded onto the pre-column. Separation was achieved by eluting from the separating column using a gradient of 3 to 37% B [A: 0.1% formic acid in water (vol/vol), B: 0.1% formic acid in ACN (vol/vol)] over a 70-min period. Subsequently, HCD-based LC-MS/MS analysis was performed. Under positive ion mode, full-scan mass spectra were acquired over the m/z range from 300 to 2000 using the Orbitrap mass analyzer with the mass resolution setting of 70,000. MS/MS fragmentation was performed in data-dependent mode, selecting the 20 most intense ions from each full-scan mass spectrum for high-energy collision-induced dissociation and MS2 analysis. MS2 spectra were acquired using the Orbitrap analyzer at a resolution setting of 17,500. Other parameters, presented in the centroid format, included an isolation window of 2.0 m/z units, default charge of 2+, normalized collision energy of 28%, maximum injection time (IT) of 50 ms, and dynamic exclusion of 20.0 s.
To identify N-glycosylation sites, LC-MS/MS analysis was conducted for 3 h using an Orbitrap Fusion LUMOS Tribrid Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the HCD method. Peptides were separated using a loading column (100 μm × 2 cm) and an in-house packed C18 separating capillary column (75 μm × 15 cm) containing Luna 3 μm C18 bulk packing material (Phenomenex). The mobile phases (A: water with 0.1% formic acid, and B: 80% ACN with 0.1% formic acid) were delivered and controlled by a Dionex Ultimate 3000 RPLC nano system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The LC gradient began at 2% B for the initial 8 min, followed by an increase from 2% to 10% B from 8 to 9 min, a further increase from 10% to 44% B from 9 to 183 min, and finally an increase from 44% to 99% B from 183 to 188 min. For samples analyzed using the Orbitrap Fusion LUMOS Tribrid Mass Spectrometer, peptide precursors were ionized using an EASY-Spray ionization source (Thermo Fisher Scientific) held at +2.0 kV compared to ground, with the inlet capillary temperature maintained at 320 °C. Survey scans of peptide precursors were collected in the Orbitrap analyzer over the range of 350-1600 Th, with an AGC target of 400,000, maximum IT of 50 ms, RF lens at 30%, and a resolution of 60,000 at 200 m/z. Monoisotopic precursor selection was enabled for peptide isotopic distributions, and precursors of z = 2 to 7 were selected for data-dependent MS/MS scans, with a cycle time of 3 s. Dynamic exclusion was set to 15 s, with a ±10 ppm window set around the precursor monoisotope. During HCD scans, automated scan range determination was enabled. Precursor ions were isolated using a 1.6 Th window with the quadrupole, while product ions were collected in the Orbitrap with the first mass of 110 Th, an AGC target of 50,000, a maximum IT of 30 ms, HCD collision energy at 30%, and a resolution of 15,000.
Results
Metabolic Labeling of Rice N-glycoproteins with GalNAz
We have previously demonstrated that GalNAz, an azido analog of GalNAc, was capable of the metabolic labeling of O-GlcNAcylated proteins in rice seedlings (
37
). In plants, including rice and
Arabidopsis
, the currently known glycans do not use GalNAc as a monosaccharide building block; however, GalNAc and UDP-GalNAc have been identified in plants (
15
,
38
,
39
,
40
). Similar to human UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE),
Arabidopsis
UDP-glucose 4-epimerases (UGEs) have been shown to catalyze the interconversion between UDP-GalNAc and UDP-
N
-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), as well as UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose (
41
,
42
). Presumably, GalNAz is metabolically converted to UDP-
N
-azidoacetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAz)
via
the same pathway in both
Arabidopsis
and rice.
By performing a BLAST analysis, we identified four highly conserved UDP-glucose 4-epimerases (OsUGE1-4) in rice that showed high homology to GALE (
Supplemental Fig. S1
). Structure alignment between the three-dimensional structures of OsUGEs predicted by AlphaFold2 (
43
) and the X-ray crystal structure of GALE (
42
) revealed a high degree of structural similarity (
Fig. 1
A
and
Supplemental Fig. S2
). Induced fit docking analysis showed that UDP-GlcNAc bound to the catalytic pocket of OsUGEs in a manner similar to the binding between UDP-GlcNAc and GALE (
44
) (
Fig. 1
B
and
Supplemental Fig. S3
). These data suggest that OsUGEs should possess a similar enzymatic activity to GALE.

N-glycoproteomic Profiling in Rice Seedlings
To comprehensively identify rice N-glycoproteins, the rice seedlings were cultured with 10 mM GalNAz or mock for 3 days (
Fig. 3
). The plants were lysed, reacted with alkyne-biotin
via
click chemistry, and enriched by streptavidin beads, followed by on-bead trypsin digestion and centrifugation. The resulting peptides in the supernatants of the experimental and control groups were labeled with isotopically heavy and light dimethyl labels, respectively, by using the reductive dimethylation method. The peptides were then analyzed by LC-MS/MS to identify N-glycosylated proteins. In parallel, the pellets of the GalNAz-treated group were treated with PNGase A and PNGase F to release N-glycopeptides from the beads. PNGase A/F cleavage converts Asn to aspartic acid (Asp), resulting in a mass shift allowing precise identification of the N-glycosylation sites (
Fig. 3
and
Supplemental Fig. S4
).

N-glycosylation is Critical for the Proper Function of ERAD-L
As shown by the KEGG pathway enrichment analysis, N-glycosylated proteins in rice were implicated in protein processing in ER (
Fig. 5
D
). The ER provides a favorable environment for protein folding (
55
). Misfolded proteins can cause ER stress, which activates the ER quality control system, leading to the removal and degradation of these proteins through the ERAD system (
56
). There are three ERAD pathways: ERAD-L handles soluble lumenal or ER lumen-extending membrane proteins, ERAD-C deals with membrane proteins in the cytosol, and ERAD-M monitors membrane proteins with misfolded domains (
56
,
57
,
58
,
59
). Studies in yeast and multicellular organisms have shed light on the mechanism of ERAD system (
60
). In yeast, the Hrd1 complex, consisting of Yos9 lectin and Hrd3 E3 ubiquitin ligase, monitors the glycosylation and folding status of most ERAD-L substrates. These substrates are processed by various enzymes, such as OST, calnexin/CALR, mannosidase, glucosidase, and protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) (
56
). ERAD is crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis and dysfunction of ERAD leads to diseases such as liver disease and Alzheimer’s disease (
61
,
62
,
63
,
64
). The ERAD machinery is conserved across various organisms, including plants (
65
,
66
,
67
). As opposed to yeast and animals, the regulatory mechanism of the ERAD machinery in plants remains largely unknown.
The key components of the ERAD-L machinery in rice, including OST complex subunit STT3B, protein disulfide isomerases (OsPDIL1-1, OsPDIL1-4, OsPDIL5-2, and OsPDIL5-4), CALR, alpha-1,2-mannosidase, Sel1/Hrd3, and OS9, were among the list of identified N-glycoproteins (
Fig. 7
A
). A subset of them was expressed in the tobacco expression system and validated as N-glycosylated proteins (
Fig. 7
B
). Furthermore, mutation of the N-glycosylation sites (both identified and predicted) of the ERAD-L components to glutamine in rice callus resulted in a decreased molecular weight in comparison to their WT counterparts, attributing to the loss of N-glycans (
Fig. 7
C
).

Discussion
Accumulating evidence has indicated that protein glycosylation, particularly N-glycosylation, plays important regulatory roles in important biological processes in rice. For example, deficiencies in OST and mannosyl-oligosaccharide glucosidase have been associated with impaired root development (
52
). Abnormality in β1,2-xylosyltransferase was found to affect rice seed germination (
51
). To further reveal the regulatory mechanisms of N-glycosylation, it is a prerequisite to identify the N-glycosylated proteins and modification sites in rice. The currently available dataset of identified rice N-glycoproteins is much smaller than those of animals and other plants (
21
,
23
,
24
,
25
). By exploring the use of MGL in N-glycoproteomic profiling in rice, this work greatly expands the rice N-glycosylation database.
The MGL-based methods have emerged as a powerful tool for glycoproteomics in various organisms, with the animal systems mostly studied (
20
). Several pioneering studies have demonstrated the applicability of MGL in plants including
A
.
thaliana
and rice (
10
,
37
). In this study, we extend the application of MGL to N-glycoproteome profiling of crops and identify 403 N-glycosylation sites and 673 N-glycosylated proteins in rice, of which 519 proteins were newly discovered. The validation of over 10 selected N-glycoproteins supports the reliability of the rice N-glycoproteomic dataset.
Mass spectrometry identified several peptides derived from rice PNGase A, where Asn was converted to Asp (
Supplemental Fig. S12
). However, as the final step in identifying N-glycosylation sites in this study involved the addition of exogenous rice PNGase A to release N-glycopeptides from the beads, it remains uncertain whether these Asn-to-Asp conversion peptides from PNGase A represent the N-glycosylation sites on endogenous rice PNGase A, even though they may represent potential N-glycosylation sites. Therefore, these PNGase A–derived peptides were excluded from the analysis of rice N-glycosylation sites in this study. The N-glycosylation sites were identified by enzymatic release of the captured N-glycopeptides containing azides incorporated into the N-glycans from the streptavidin beads by PNGase A/F cleavage. The Asn residues may also undergo nonenzymatic deamidation, resulting in the Asn-to-Asp conversion (
71
). In the MGL-based profiling of N-glycosylation sites in rice, the capture of N-glycopeptides hinged on the presence of azide-incorporated glycans, and PNGase A & F–based enzymatic cleavage ensured that the released peptides were from N-glycopeptides. The PNGase A & F–catalyzed Asn-to-Asp conversion was used as a further validation of the N-glycosylation sites. To assess whether nonenzymatic deamidation interfered with the identification of N-glycosylation sites, we performed a proteomic analysis on rice seedlings, in which 853 out of the total 59,156 peptides underwent nonenzymatic deamidation (
Supplemental Table S5
). Notably, only five of them overlapped with the identified N-glycosylation sites (
Supplemental Fig. S13
), accounting for 1.2% of the identified N-glycosylation sites. Among the five overlapping N-glycosylation sites, three conformed to the canonical motif Asn-X-Ser/Thr. This suggests that while nonenzymatic deamidation may introduce a minimal number of false positives in identifying N-glycosylation sites using the MGL-based method, it does not significantly affect the overall results.
N-glycosylation plays important roles in rice growth and yield. For instance, cytokinins are essential plant hormones that regulate rice growth and development. The endogenous levels of cytokinins are controlled by cytokinin oxidase/dehydrogenase (CKX). Quantitative trait locus analysis indicates that a locus responsible for grain yield, Gn1a, encodes OsCKX2 (
72
). Reduced expression of
OsCKX2
increased the number of panicles per plant, total grain number per plant, and total grain weight per plant. Importantly, the enzymatic activity of OsCKX2 was correlated with its N-glycosylation (
73
). Altering the N-glycosylation site sequence of OsCKX2 can increase tiller number and grain weight, thereby improving rice yield. Additionally, knocking out
OsPML3
, a gene that regulates the late-stage Golgi N-glycosylation, led to dwarfism, necrosis of root tips and lateral root primordia, chlorosis in young leaves, reduced pollen fertility, and decreased grain yield, while overexpression of
OsPML3
significantly increased the root length and shoot height (
74
). The root is essential for water and nutrient absorption in rice, directly affecting the yield. A mutation in DGL1, a subunit of the rice OST complex, resulted in impaired N-glycosylation, causing root development defects. Overexpression of
DGL1
in the mutant significantly increased the root length (
75
). In this study, we found that another subunit of the OST complex, STT3b, is also N-glycosylated. Manipulating the N-glycosylation on STT3b may lead to a means to regulate the root development and improve the rice yield.
The rice N-glycoproteins identified are involved in various important biological processes, such as metabolism and stress response. The ERAD machinery plays a critical role in degrading unassembled or misfolded proteins in the ER and is involved in regulating important biological processes in rice, such as grain size and resistance to blast disease (
76
). A few ERAD-L components including OST and PDIs were previously identified to be N-glycosylated (
23
,
24
